text: Where step 1 stands, plainly. BUILT, pushed at 73623c6: appFaceApp on the VPS takes a visitor's request, asks your box once 'who owns this host?', remembers the answer, and forwards the request. Your box answers from grants.json and, for a name it owns, sends back the agreed 'not served yet' (501, naming your node). One piece is missing for your box to say 'mine': it must know its own key, which is api.self(), included in wsl-claude's go-ask above. HOW IT'S TESTED, two ways: (1) in the lab, which wsl-claude is writing: a relay, your node with 'join' granted to itself, a puppet node with the face on. A plain HTTP request for join.face.spirit.test must come back with your node's key in it, a second request must not ask your box again, and an unknown name must get 'no such route'. (2) LIVE, after the VPS setup: open https://join.face.spirit.andyflinn.com in your browser and you should see 'last-leg-not-built' with your node's key. That's the proof you asked for, the route to the owner and back. The live one needs the Caddy setup on the VPS first (DreamHost key, one block), which is in the same go.

Yours, and I'm standing down. What the scripts need from the code side: (1) the Caddy block for face.spirit.<domain> and *.face.spirit.<domain>, reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<face port>, with a tls block using dns dreamhost {env.DREAMHOST_API_KEY} (the caddy-dns/dreamhost module; the key in a root-only env file for the caddy unit, never in the repo). Follow bash/tls's one-file-per-domain rule: write /etc/caddy/sites/face.spirit.<domain>.caddy, never touch the main Caddyfile. (2) On the VPS puppet node: relay-state/face.json { "port": <face port> } turns puppetPost on (puppetPost.js faceConfigIn), and appFaceApp boots there (manifest boots:true, already set). It claims the face when the node hands it api.face. (3) On Andy's node, not the VPS: app/appFaceApp/face-domain.json { "faceDomain": "face.spirit.andyflinn.com" }, and the grants.json row for join to his node's key. That's his side, maybe a small script for him too. The caddy binary needs the module: xcaddy build --with github.com/caddy-dns/dreamhost, or Caddy's download page.

The node itself has always had it: its identity (public and private key) lives in relay-state/identity.json, and every post the node sends is signed with it (peerPost.js, 'me()' at the top of post). What's walled off is the APP running inside the node, appFaceApp. When it calls api.post, the node signs on its behalf, so the app never holds the private key, by design. api.self() would hand the app only the node's PUBLIC key, the same one every node's card already gives to anybody. appFaceApp needs it only to recognise its own key in a grant row, 'this name is granted to me'. It can't sign anything with it.

Only to let your node say 'mine', and your question shows we don't need it. Simpler: your node doesn't judge. It just answers truthfully 'the owner of join is <key>', straight from grants.json. The puppet already knows its own owner's key (puppet.json). If the answer is that key, it forwards to your node; otherwise it's someone else's, the redirect case, later. And the stub your node sends back names the key from the row, which is your own. So api.self() is dropped: no widening of the app interface at all. I'll change it now.

Andy's question removes api.self(). The owner node answers { route:'owner', name, to: <row.to> } with no self-judging; the puppet compares 'to' with api.owner() and forwards to its owner when they match (the 'mine' case). The stub 501 names node = row.to. So your go-ask's api.self() part can be ignored. Changing it now.

Before I write the VPS scripts, two things I found change them. This replaces my earlier Go on this row (same step 1, plus these two).
(1) THE DREAMHOST ROUTE DOESN'T WORK TODAY. Caddy needs a plug-in to talk to DreamHost, and Caddy's own download service refuses to build it: 'unable to fulfill download request', on every version I tried, while the same request with Cloudflare's plug-in builds fine. BETTER, and simpler: certificates ON DEMAND. Your DNS already sends every *.face.spirit name to the VPS. Caddy can fetch a certificate for each name the first time it's visited, after asking our face 'is this name real?'. So no DreamHost key on the VPS, and only names your node actually granted ever get a certificate.
(2) A SECOND PROGRAM ON THE VPS. The face runs in a small SpiritOS node (the 'puppet') on the VPS, next to the relay. bash/README.md says that box runs ONE Node process, the relay, and 'never' a personal node. So the rule changes: the relay plus the puppet node, and still nothing else. Cost: roughly 50-80 MB of the 1 GB.
Go = step 1 as before (claude-windows wires it, I prove it in a lab world), with on-demand certificates, the puppet node allowed on the VPS, and I write the ./bash/ scripts for that and update the README's rule. No = hold. If only one part is a No, say which.
